10036776:
Dawson Julia Winslow LD 584
Hello members of the VLA committee -
My name is Dawson Julia and I live in Winslow Maine and am a very active advocate of medical cannabis as well as Adult Use. I am also the founding member of Maine Cannabis Coalition a group that was formed in August of 2016 and the reason I created that Non-profit corporation has a lot of reasoning to explain why I am completely in support of LD584. Please consider this my written testimony in full support of LD 584
It's a long story but after you read this I'm sure you will understand and if you have any questions please don't hesitate to ask me questions.
It was August 3rd of 2016 and as I looked out my window across the street to the Unity country store I could see a Waldo county sheriff truck was parked for what I thought was a lunch break. Shortly after a few moments there were 3 more sheriff trucks coming down the road and I watched as the 4th truck joined the other trucks and I remember getting really excited because everyone in town knew that there was a pill house 5 places down the road from my place and Naturally I thought they were finally gonna get busted!
To provide a little more background at the time I was the only caregiver storefront in the state. There were 8 dispensary licenses issued at the time and in 2008 we voted for medical marijuana to be legal but after the state issued all 8 licenses only 1 native Mainer received a license and the rest were out of staters or freshly moved to Maine. In 2016 6 dispensary licenses were owned by what I call Corporate Cannabis (trade on the stock market) but yet it was illegal for a caregiver to have a partner or partners.
I started East Coast CBDs in 2012 and I thought soon there would be a lot of caregiver stores and appartently there wasn't and I think a lot of folks were watching me and waiting to see when I would get busted. Between 2012 and 2015 I had 2 inspections and everytime there was always a conversation from the inspector about how it was illegal to have a caregiver storefront. So my message to the inspector was "you tell Marietta (Director from 2010-2016) that if she wants to violate me I'll gladly go in front of a judge with alot of elderly patients testfying for me about how I'm the only place in Maine to sell non pyschoactive CBD marijuanna in the state and I got beyond a reasonable doubt on my side."
Apparently the message got through to Marietta because on August 3rd of 2016 she came to my place with a total of 5 Waldo County Sheriff's trucks and they were coming for me not the "pill house". The big problelm was I was stealing a lot of patients from "corporate cannabis" and Marietta went out of her way to help them on a regular basis. In fact she planned this out because it was clearly a criminal investigation not a inspection and they thought they were taking my plants away with all those trucks. You see August 3rd was the same day my wife "Kellie's" caregiver card expired!
When the investigation was almost over Marietta asked to see the 2 caregiver cards. When I gave her Kellie's card she was very quick to point out that it had expired. So I said to Marietta in front of all the deputy's and my employees "let me check the mail because I mailed it in about 2 months ago. Marietta replied "don't bother" I said why shouldn't I she replied "lets just say it came accross my desk" while she winked at me
After a brief discusion of if it expired last night at 12:01AM or if it expired tonight at 12:01AM Then I had a ureeka moment! You see at the time we were training my stepson (Corey) to be a caregiver but he wasn't growing any plants at the time. So what I did was grabed Corey's caregiver cards and explained to Marietta that "all those plants marked K upstairs don't stand for Kellie they stand for Corey".
After everybody left I phoned a complaint to sheriff Trafton of Waldo county who

was a democrat and at the time Lepage was our governor and appointed Marietta. To my surprise sheriff Trafton was not aware that his deputy's were escorting Marietta and that 5 of his trucks were assisting.
In 2015 my place was robbed for about $50,000 worth of plants and at the time they didn't have the "resources" to even do fingerprints but apparently they had the resources to distribute 5 trucks and deputies to go with them to assist on A inspection for a caregiver that had no violations on record. So I stated this and asked sheriff Trafton why I shouldn't contact the press and tell them everything.
To make a long story short Marietta was fired a week later.
Then eventually Director Eric Gunderson had taken over and he was appointed by Governor Mills. I had several meetings with Director Gunderson and I stressed each time to look after the locals and if anybody needs to be harrased I recomended corporate cannabis.
In 2022 Director Gunderson resigned and one of the last things he did the day before he resigned is send a memorandium out to all the caregivers that said for now on if you sell vape pens, prerolls, pipes, roling papers or even lighters you need to have a tobacco license. To explain a little more history to make it easier to understand there was a bill in 2020 that would have made it law that you had to be a dispensary to sell vape pens,pipes even rolling papers and it failed misserably but the dispensaries already had their tobacco licenses so they didn't get A law but they got a memorandium. This was clearly a farewell gift to corporate cannabis.
Eventually Gunderson was replaced by Hudak and I could write a book for the problems Hudak has been for the locals. A petition was started in 2024 to fire Hudak and it got over 1,000 signatures but sadly nothing was done by the one person who could take action (our govenor).
On top of a serious petition that is getting ignored Hudak is also under investigation by the government oversite comittee. OCP clearly needs legislative guidance to appoint the next director before another incident occurs. I beg you to vote in favor of this bill and add another layer of protection to the locals.
Best Regards Dawson Julia
10035682:
Duncan Markovich Better Ways LLC - Branford, CT LD 584
To Chairs Senator Hickman and Representative Supica, and all esteemed members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee,
I appreciate this opportunity today to share with you my support for LD 584.
My name is Duncan Markovich, owner and founder of Better Ways, a cannabis therapeutics, education, and community center in my hometown of Branford, CT.
I use cannabis daily for pain management and nerve damage after a surgical complication resulting from my 4th open heart surgery in 2010.
My grandfather flew for the Navy as a Hurricane Hunter and I have the greatest respect for those that assist our veterans with accessing the quality cannabis they deserve, so thank you truly for what this committee does and stands for.
Today I wanted to aid my colleague and fellow cannabis activist Derek Shirley with echoing the need for fair and objective appointments of any official, government or not, when it comes to the oversight affairs of anything cannabis related.
As this plant and its attached industry continues to expand in concept and practice, we must ensure overall integrity and transparency by collaborative design - without those bearings and guardrails, the plant and ultimately those that rely on it are put in harm's way.
In this case harm has occurred in the form of significant broken trust, both at the state level and within our cannabis community in Maine and here in New England.
I feel this bill will strengthen the needed transparency when appointing such regulatory officials and begin repairing faith and trust in the Office of Cannabis Policy. More importantly I feel that this bill provides a beacon towards the telos of improvement and integrity for our region to take note of.
I also feel it prudent to take this moment and remind those currently overseeing regulation and enforcement around cannabis that it is a great privilege to work alongside this plant and our community. As an industry, we are a highly self-regulating network of healers, professionals, farmers, activists and patients which is why having these conversations with our elected officials is tantamount when designing ethical and equitable cannabis laws.
When there is a potential danger to the sanctity of this balance within our community, whether it be by an individual, brand, operator, regulator or legislator...we are unflinching to raise the appropriate concerns as well as offer equally appropriate solutions and support.
I commend the great state of Maine and this committee for its continued commitment to these tenets - I feel that effort is also well exemplified in your medical cannabis caregiver model. Some of its language has been successfully adopted into our own Connecticut Caregiver Bill - HB 5429 which thankfully has gained much momentum this session, so from one state with its own cannabis conundrum, thank you for giving us a pragmatic framework to create solutions.
It is in this very moment we are sharing right now; this is where democracy lives and breathes when there is a thoughtful discord between community members, patients, activists, and legislators. Please aid us in continued protection and liberty for this great plant and those it serves.
Free the plant, free the people.
I welcome any questions or comments.
Duncan Markovich - Owner and Founder - Better Ways LLC - Branford, CT

STATE OF MAINE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE & FINANCIAL SERVICES
BURTON M. CROSS BUILDING, 3RD FLOOR 78 STATE HOUSE STATION AUGUSTA, MAINE 04333-0078

SERVING THE PUBLIC AND DELIVERING ESSENTIAL SERVICES TO STATE GOVERNMENT

JANET T. MILLS GOVERNOR

KIRSTEN LC FIGUEROA COMMISSIONER

LD 584 An Act to Make the Director of the Office of Cannabis Policy an Appointed Position Subject to Confirmation by the Legislature
Testimony of Kirsten LC Figueroa
March 10, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs. I am Kirsten Figueroa, Commissioner of the Department of Administrative and Financial Services (DAFS). I am providing this testimony in opposition to LD 584.
DAFS is a comprehensive department, consisting of ten divisions and more than 1,400 positions. DAFS employees are respected as conscientious stewards of the State's assets: fiscal, human, physical and technical. We are valued for the professional expertise we provide. We lead and collaborate with open doors, open minds, and open hearts.
The DAFS Commissioner "may appoint and employ deputy commissioners, bureau chiefs and the director of legislative affairs [as well as an associate commissioner for administrative services, associate commissioner of Tax Policy, Director of Compliance], to be under the commissioner's immediate supervision, direction and control, and to serve at the commissioner's pleasure and perform such duties as the commissioner may prescribe, except as otherwise provided by law". Of the fourteen appointments, eight are Bureau leads, including the Director of Cannabis Policy.
This bill proposes that one of the fourteen appointed positions in DAFS, one of the eight Bureau chiefs, the Director of Cannabis Policy, rather than serving at the pleasure of the Commissioner of the department that houses the cannabis policy office, be appointed by the Governor, and, like the Governor's Cabinet appointments which this position is not, be subject to legislative review and confirmation. Furthermore, it implements this change nearly immediately.
It is unclear why this bureau director-level position, among the many in DAFS and the dozens of those designated as major policy-influencing in state government, should be singled out this way, and the Department is concerned about what it would mean for the long-term stability of OCP.
I would like to express to the Committee that the staff at OCP are a group of professionals who have been working their best within a new and still evolving policy space to effectively and fairly regulate Maine's adult use and medical cannabis industries as set forth by statute.

PHONE: (207) 624-7800

www.Maine.gov

FAX: (207) 624-7804

For the last six years, since the establishment of the Office in February of 2019, the OCP team has been incredibly dedicated and instrumental to figuring this out with you, for cannabis businesses, consumers, and patients, and for communities across the State.
The Office is currently led by Director John Hudak, a nationally recognized expert in cannabis policy who has worked in the space since the first states began legalizing recreational cannabis. Prior to joining OCP, Director Hudak served as Deputy Director of the Center for Effective Public Management and as a Senior Fellow in Governance Studies at the Brookings Institution, an esteemed nonprofit public policy organization based in Washington, DC. He led Brookings' research into cannabis policy, regulation, implementation, and politics for over 10 years. In addition, Director Hudak previously served as a consultant to numerous state and local governments, helping them design and improve their cannabis rules and regulations. His vast experience and qualifications are why he was recruited and appointed Director of OCP, and we are lucky to have him.
The Director of OCP position has always been subject to scrutiny, as have cannabis regulators across the country--it is not unique to Director Hudak. Director Hudak has always been clear and transparent about his past working relationships prior to joining OCP, both during the hiring process and publicly since he started in his role. And, Director Hudak's required financial disclosure statements, publicly available online, show he has no direct or indirect pecuniary interest in the state's cannabis operating systems, including Metrc. The State of Maine entered into a six-year contract with its current vendor Metrc in February 2020, three years before Director Hudak came to work for the State of Maine. That contract ends in February 2026 and is currently out for competitive bid.
This position is the kind that is already challenging to fill with well-qualified candidates, and adding legislative confirmation to the process is likely to discourage some from considering the position. This concern is heightened by the fact that Maine's regulated cannabis industry continues to operate adjacent to a large illicit market. An extended vacancy at the leadership level would undermine the state's cannabis policy direction as well as impact the long-term stability of OCP, a relatively young state agency that has performed admirably while navigating a unique, ever-changing policy space.
We respectfully urge Committee members to vote LD 584 ought not to pass and to maintain parity between the appointment of OCP's Director with that of directors at DAFS and throughout agencies across State government.
This concludes my testimony. Thank you.

Leo Paquette Firefly Organics/Cannabis Guild of Maine LD 584
Good Morning, Esteemed members of the VLA committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to submit written testimony as I regretfully can't be there in person. I am writing to you today to express my strong support for LD584. I have been a licensed cannabis operator since 2011. We currently employ 34 people across 3 companies including retail, manufacturing, and cultivation.
The cannabis industry in Maine has grown significantly in recent years, and with this growth comes and increased need for strong leadership, transparency, and accountability within the Office of Cannabis Policy. By making the Director of this office an appointed position, subject to legislative confirmation, Operators AND consumers can ensure that the individual selected for this critical role has the qualifications, experience, and public trust necessary to effectively manage the state's cannabis program.
There are several key reasons why I believe LD 584 is essential:
1.) Increased Accountability: Making the Director of OCP subject to confirmation by the legislature will ensure that the individual holding this position is accountable not only to the Governor but also to the people of Maine through their elected representatives. This process will foster greater transparency in the election process and ensure that the Director remains responsive to the needs of all stakeholders in the cannabis industry, including businesses, consumers, and local communities. 2.) Public Trust and Confidence: The cannabis industry is still relatively new in Maine, and I have concerns about the regulatory framework and how the industry is being managed. We should have a Director who supports our growing industry and all I have seen from our current Director is questionable actions at best. By subjecting the Directors appointment to legislative confirmation, Maines citizens can have more confidence that the Director is not only qualified but also has the support of the legislative body that represents us. This process will help instill trust in the regulatory process and in the policies governing cannabis. 3.) Expert Leadership: The cannabis industry is complex, and its regulations are constantly evolving. By ensuring that the Director is appointed through a formal process, the legislature can evaluate the qualifications and track record of the candidate. This ensures that the Director is equipped with the knowledge and experience necessary to oversee the states cannabis program effectively and adapt to the changing landscape of the industry. 4.) Checks and Balances: One of the fundamental principles of our democracy is the system of checks and balances. The confirmation process provides and additional layer of oversight and helps prevent the concentration of power in the hands of single individual or a single branch of government. It ensures the that the Director is accountable to both the executive and legislative branches and ultimately, to the people of Maine.
In conclusion, LD 584 represents an important step toward ensuring that Maines cannabis program is managed with transparency, accountability, and expertise.By making the Director of OCP an appointed position subject to confirmation, we can create a more balanced, effective, and trusted regulatory system. I strongly urge you to support this important piece of legislation and look forward to seeing the positive impact it will have on Maines cannabis industry and the citizens it serves.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have at any time.
Sincerely, Leo Paquette Firefly Organics/Fire on Fore/Cannabis Guild of Maine Cell: 207-650-8759 Email: Leo@ffomaine.com

10036441:
Mark Barnett Policy Director, Maine Craft Cannabis Association
To the Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, March 10th, 2025
LD 584: OUGHT TO PASS
My name is Mark Barnett. I'm a resident of Auburn, the owner of an Adult Use retail store in Portland, and the Policy Director for the Maine Craft Cannabis Association. On behalf of our Association I am submitting this testimony in favor of LD 584: An Act to Make the Director of the Office of Cannabis Policy an Appointed Position Subject to Confirmation by the Legislature. In our view, this bill is part of the evolution of our relationship with the cannabis plant following legalization, as we move away from stigma and away from economies--both commercial and political--built around its prohibition.
At present, the regulatory environment and the ecosystem of `experts' that have captured that environment in the cannabis industry are uniquely skewed away from `plant-touching' real-world experience with cannabis and skewed towards policing and restricting the activity of citizens and businesses even in `legal' states. In short, nobody in the positions of power has any experience with the actual business of cannabis. This bill will directly help to address that by introducing a strong voice for the people in the choice of leadership for our current regulatory institutions.
We see no impetus for this situation to change so long as the Executive Branch enjoys widesweeping powers over the fundamental, day-to-day lives of cannabis businesses and consumers. These powers over so many of our industry's activities--concentrated in the hands of just a few--are uniquely unchecked. Further, with the excuse that the plant is federally illegal, attempts to democratize the policies of this industry are met with stiff resistance and at times institutional disdain.
This is a product, in our view, of the lack of public participation in these key conversations, and of the lack of oversight from the people's Legislature. It is a large part of why advocates, as small businesses and consumers, have to volunteer so much time and energy every year to fight so many battles big and small through the legislative process. Our regulators are distant from public opinion and often hostile towards our input in the regulation of our industry. This creates an antagonistic environment which, fundamentally, doesn't work well for the industry, the consumer, or the State of Maine.

While there is no `silver bullet', someday we certainly won't need an Office of Cannabis Policy. It should and shall be regulated as the varying different types of commerce contained within it: agriculture, retail, manufacturing, baking, staffing, transport, etc. Until we get to that day, however, we certainly don't need to place such potent weapons in the hands of those that staff the OCP nor in the hands of people who view their job as controlling a `dangerous' problem. `Cannabis' is neither dangerous nor new. We ought to stop relying on `experts' steeped in the prohibition-era attitudes of the past and bring a little more democracy into these conversations to reflect that.
Sincerely,
Mark Barnett Maine Craft Cannabis Association
185296:
March 10, 2025

LD 584

Matthew K Bayliss Gele LLC
South Portland Maine

Good morning, Chair and committee members. My name is Matthew Bayliss. I'm a
Cumberland resident, a registered caregiver for over ten years, and I recently
surrendered my adult-use cultivation license under duress. I'm here to testify in
support of LD 584, requiring Senate approval for the OCP Director. Six weeks after the
Office of Cannabis Policy launched under Director Gunderson, I began dozens of
candid conversations with them about how small businesses could navigate new rules, regulations, taxes, and burdens. When the market opened in October 2020, I was one
of the first licensees--and one of the smallest. Within months, I warned them their system would crush small operators. They agreed, promised revisions to ease the load,
but never delivered.
That load hit hard with Metrc, the track-and-trace system--sloppy, with poor customer service, and too expensive to maintain. It's a key reason I left the program. I raised this
in multiple stakeholder meetings with OCP higher-ups. Their response? `We don't like Metrc either, but they're our vendor--what can we do?' That's not accountability; it's resignation. Meanwhile, Metrc's pocketed nearly a million dollars from OCP contracts tmder John Hudak, the current director. Hudak co-founded Freedman & Koski, a firm that consulted for Maine--one partner's now at Metrc. The other, Andrew Freedman,
created CPEAR in D.C., lobbying for giants like Altria--big tobacco betting on cannabis. Hudak himself worked at CPEAR before coming to Maine to lead OCP.
Maine law demands avoiding even the *appearance* of a conflict. When your past ties
profit from decisions crushing small growers, and D.C. lobbyists for corporate heavyweights loom, that's a red flag. Altria isn't here for caregivers--they want market control. Senate approval could've vetted this: Are you here for Maine's small operators or corporate boardrooms? Right now, it feels like the latter. Fees, rules, Metrc's costs-
they favor big players, not the little guys and gals who built this industry, many
testifying before you today.
The OCP Director wields huge power: contracts, regulations, livelihoods. Senate
oversight ensures they answer to us, not just the governor. Trust's low--see the `Fire
John Hudak' movement or the Oversight Committee's probe. My story's proof: promises broken, small businesses sidelined, a system rigged for scale. LD 584 is about fairness--giving Maine's cannabis community a voice in who leads us. It's a chance to
stop corporate creep and protect what we've built. Please vote yes. I'd be happy to answer any questions. Thank you.
10036329:
Paul McCarrier Monroe LD 584
Good morning Chairman Hickman, Chairwoman Suppica and honorable members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs committee, my name is Paul T. McCarrier and I operate a vertically integrated medical cannabis company in Mid-Coast Maine. I am testifying in support of LD 584 "An Act to Make the Director of the Office of Cannabis Policy an Appointed Position Subject to Confirmation by the Legislature".
I believe this bill is an important step forward in restoring trust between the regulated community and the Office of Cannabis Policy. Frankly, trust is at an all time low and there is a distinct lack of confidence in the current leadership of OCP. If there was more trust, I believe you would see more support from the community for OCPs legislative agenda, such as mandatory testing and more regulations. From dozens of conversations with community members, there is no trust that under current leadership OCP would follow legislative intent on new legislation or listen to community feedback.
The way that OCP top leadership has implemented new legislation seems to ignore the intent of your committee and the greater legislature. Though it was approved into law last year, there still is no "one click" renewal for annual registrations. This leads to addiontal work for small businesses that do not have law firms that do this for them, and takes away from the day to day operations providing for their patients and customers.
While I do not participate in the Adult Use program, there are frequent complaints about additonal requirements that continue to be piled on these businesses. These include additonal testing requirements, which sometimes comes not from an OCP guidance document, but from the tracking vendor METRC. This raises the question of who is deciding this policy, the company METRC or OCP leadership. Or are they one and the same?
While the rank and file have become easier to work with, the leadership at OCP seems to take a hostile stance against the community they regulate. There is constant fear about retribution if you speak out. There is the feeling that OCP does not want many of these small, mom and pop businesses to succeed, based upon actions such as a $2,500 late fee for application renewal and additonal inspections for "troublemakers".
This lack of trust has been building for years and was not as serious under the previous director, Erik Gunderson. Under Gundersons leadership, there was the feeling that OCP wanted to see the program grow and succeed. There was hope that under the current director, this would continue and grow. There is palpable disappointment this has not occurred. I believe if this bill was law when a new director was being sought, the Senate and greater legislature would have been able to divine the intent, have important questions answered, and there would have been some sort of accountability for OCP leadership.
For the reasons explained above, I'm asking you to support and vote ought to pass on LD 584. Thank you for your attention to this important bill and I'm happy to answer any questions.
